subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO STUDY PROBLEM OF INSTITUTING CANADIAN SYSTEM
REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO STUDY PROBLEM OF INSTITUTING CANADIAN SYSTEM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I .beg leave to present the second and final report of the special committee on radio broadcasting also a copy of the proceedings and evidence. Further, I wish to give notice that on Wednesday I shall move for concurrence. The report is as follows:
Monday, May 9, 1932.
The special committee on radio broadcasting has the honour to present the following as its second and final report:
In accordance with the duties and responsibilities delegated to us, and the terms of reference submitted, your committee met on March 8, and, since that time, held twenty-seven meetings, heard evidence, received briefs and submissions from fifty-three sources, including governments, individuals, corporations, associations, leagues and clubs.
Your committee was seized, from the inception, of the national importance and international character of radio broadcasting, and the evidence submitted has ser%Ted to further consolidate our opinion of the far-reaching scope and benefits of proper, well-regulated broadcasting services throughout Canada, as a medium of education, thought-provoking development, and fostering of Canadian ideals and culture, entertainment, news service and publicity of this country and its products, and as an auxiliary to religious and educational teaching, also as one of the most efficient mediums for developing a greater national and empire consciousness within the dominion and the British Commonwealth of nations.
Your committee desires to express at the outset, to the present radio broadcasting stations, this tribute: That they entered as pioneers in a field of service in the art of radio, and, under trying handicaps and sacrifices, worthily kept pace with a science fraught with ever-changing improvements and development, and rendered this service under handicaps, which is most praiseworthy.
Radio-Report of Committee

Your committee is convinced, however, that the present system, excellent as it is in certain respects, does not meet the requirements in quality and scope of broadcasting to ensure its maximum benefits.
Reference No. 1
"To consider the report of the Royal Commission on Radio Broadcasting, dated the 11th day of September, 1929, commonly known as 'The Aird report/ "
Your committee was fortunate in having the three members of the Aird commission appear before us to amplify and explain their report, and much valuable information was thereby secured, and, if we are unable to completely accept their findings, it must be obvious that there has been a great change in the science of radio broadcasting, and in the financial condition of the country, in the last three years.
Reference No. 2
"To advise and recommend a complete technical scheme for radio broadcasting for Canada, so designed as to ensure from Canadian sources as complete and satisfactory a service as the present development of radio science will permit."
Your committee recommends a chain of high-power national stations, operating on clear channels, located at suitable intervals, the location to be determined by a careful technical survey of Canada.
Your committee recommends that consideration be given to the use of five 50 K.W. stations, one in each of the following provinces of Canada, viz., British Columbia, Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec, and, in the maritimes, three 500 watt stations, one for each province, or one 50 K.W. station, as may be determined by the commission. In Saskatchewan and Alberta, we suggest two 5 KW. stations in each province, synchronized on a common channel. Further, a 10 K.W. station in northern Ontario and one in western Ontario, a 1 K.W. station at Port Arthur-Fort William, a 500 watt station in Toronto, and a 1 K.W. station at, or near, Ottawa, Montreal and Quebec.
Your committee further recommends a number of stations, of 100 watt power and under, operating on shared channels, located where required,-
(a)	To serve areas not satisfactorily covered by the national stations.
(b)	For secondary stations in areas where there is a demand for several channels to be in operation at the same time.
(c)	For educational purposes.
fd) For legitimate experimental work.
(e)	For local broadcasting of community interest.
Your committee further recommends that the cost of radio in Canada be self-sustaining and that only the money available from transmitters' and receivers' licence fees, and advertising income, be expended, and that the question of the amount of receivers' licence fees be left entirely in the hands of the governor in council.
Reference No. 3
"To investigate and report upon the most satisfactory agency for carrying out such a scheme."

Your committee recommends that a commission be appointed, consisting of three adequately-paid coriimissioners; a chairman to hold office for a period of ten years; a vicechairman for a period of nine years, and the third commissioner, for a period of eight years.
That there be appointed an assistant commissioner in each province, who shall also act as chairman of such provincial or regional advisory program committees as may be formed; the assistant commissioners to be selected in consultation with the governments of their respective provinces.
Your committee further recommends that the commission be vested with the necessary powers to carry on the business of broadcasting in the Dominion of Canada, such powers to extend to the following matters,-
(a)	To regulate and control all broadcasting in Canada, including programs and advertising.
(b)	To own, build and operate transmitting or receiving stations in Canada.
(c)	To acquire by lease, purchase, expropriation or otherwise, any or all existing broadcasting stations.
(d)	To enter into operating agreements with privately-owned stations.
(e)	To originate programs, and secure outside programs by purchase or exchange, and to make the arrangements necessary for their transmission.
(f)	To determine the number, location and power of all broadcasting stations required in Canada.
(g)	To control the issuing or cancellation of licences to broadcasting stations.
(h)	To cancel the allotments of channels to any stations, or to make substitution of channels.
(i)	To prohibit the establishment of privately-operated chains of stations in Canada.
(j)	Subject to the approval of the parliament of Canada, to take over all broadcasting in Canada.
(k)	To be vested with all other powers necessary or incidental for the fulfilment of the objects of the commission.
Your committee recommends,-
(a)	That one of the first duties of the commission be the establishment of trans-Canada chain broadcasting through the securing of the necessary landmines as soon as possible.
(b)	That a nationally-owned system of radio broadcasting be instituted, and that all stations required for its proper organization be eventually acquired, same to be financed from the revenues accruing to the business of broadcasting, without expense to the taxpayers through the public treasury.
(c)	That all stations, 100 watt and under, not required for the national system, remain under private ownership, but be regulated as to programs and advertising, by the rules of the commission.
(d)	That all revenues obtained from licence fees, sale of advertisement, and other revenues accessory to the business of broadcasting, be used by the commission in the interest of radio.
(e)	That advertising be limited to not more than 5 per cent of each program period.
(f)	That the developing of Canadian art and artists, and the securing of outstanding programs from outside Canada, be encouraged.

Radio-Report of Committee
(g)	That the commission make available to the provinces, when possible, the facilities of national and chain broadcasting.
(h)	That the commission make special effort to give such programs as will be acceptable to provincial and local requirements.
(i)	That before making changes in Canadian radio broadcasting, the commission makes a complete survey of the present system, with particular reference to adequate coverage.
We desire to call attention to the extreme importance that the commission should not assume, or even be suspected of assuming, a political complexion. Your committee append hereto a copy of the proceedings, and evidence adduced before your committee, for the information of the house.
All which is respectfully submitted.
(Sgd.) Raymond D. Morand, Chairman, W. A. Beynon,
Onesime Gagnon,
R. K. Smith,
I). McK. Wright,
P. J. Cardin,
W. D. Euler,
J. L. Ilsley,

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO STUDY PROBLEM OF INSTITUTING CANADIAN SYSTEM
speechtext:
The report tabled contains a
recommendation for a technical scheme of broadcasting-pursuant to the terms of reference-which involved the employment of an increased number of channels of prescribed power, located within certain areas.
One of the outstanding difficulties in the establishment of a national system of broadcasting is that of coordinating the channels to be used with those used by neighbouring countries. Because of Canada's proximity to the United States, where a highly developed system of broadcasting prevails, this question of coordination and adjustment becomes one of peculiar importance. Having regard to this situation, and with a view to determining whether this recommendation of the committee could, in fact, be implemented without involving interference which would make it ineffective in practice, the chairman asked me, as Minister of External Affairs, to ascertain from the United States government if it was prepared to make such adjustments of channels in the broadcast band as would ensure the effective operation of the scheme. Thereupon, I requested the Canadian minister to initiate negotiations to that end. The notes which I shall read disclose the agreements which have followed upon these negotiations. I have only to add that the note of the United States government manifests a friendly desire to facilitate the effective development of the national project recommended by the committee.
The note from the Canadian minister to Mr. W. R. Castle, the Acting Secretary of State, Washington, dated Canadian Legation, Washington, May 5, 1932, reads:
Sir,
I have the honour to inform you that the Canadian House of Commons recently appointed a committee to enquire into the whole position of radio broadcasting in Canada. This committee has under consideration a technical scheme for broadcasting in Canada which it is considered will provide satisfactory coverage in the chief population areas throughout the dominion and at the same time make provision for the community service that may be desired. This scheme is divided into two distinct parts:
(a)	A chain of high-power stations, operating on clear channels, and located at suitable intervals across Canada:
(b)	A number of low-power stations of very limited range, operating on shared channels, and located as required for community service.
If this scheme receives the approval of parliament, it is proposed to use 50 K.W. stations, one in each of the provinces of British Columbia, Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec, and eventually one in the maritime provinces. In Saskatchewan and Alberta it is proposed to use 5 K.W. stations at present, two being used in each province, synchronized on a common channel. In Ontario there will be, in addition, two 10 K.W. stations, one in western Ontario-and one in northern Ontario. Four smaller stations of one K.W. capacity each are provided for the Port Arthur-Fort William area, and for Ottawa, Montreal, and Quebec. In the maritimes, three 500-watt stations are provided for the present, one in each province. The scheme also includes a 500-watt station on the shared channels for the city of Toronto for local service.
In adopting this plan, Canada would reserve the right to increase the power of the stations in Alberta, Saskatchewan, northern and western Ontario to 50 K.W. each, should such increase become necessary.
The committee, in addition to considering the power required, propose the following channels
as suitable for the main stations:

In order to ensure satisfactory local broadcast service throughout Canada, it is proposed that stations, limited to a maximum power of 100 watts, be erected where necessary, and that they should be operated on shared channels. It is considered that one hundred or more such stations may eventually be required in Canada, and that twenty channels should be available for this type of service. In establishing such stations, it is proposed to maintain the same geographical separation between Canadian and United States stations as is maintained between United States stations of the same power.
Questions

Due notification would, of course, be given of the effective dates of any changes in the present operation to conform with the above plan.
In the event of the adoption of the above arrangement, it is understood that if, as the result of the Madrid conference, any additional channels are made available for broadcasting, a further allocation will be made, as between the United States and Canada, on an equitable basis.
I shall be obliged if you will inform me at your early convenience whether the United States authorities can make the necessary readjustments so that these channels will be available for effective use in Canada.
I have the honour to be, with the highest consideration,
Sir,
Your most obedient, humble servant,
(Sgd.) W. D. Herridge.
To which Mr. Castle, Acting Secretary of State, replied under date of May 5, 1932:
Sir,-
I am grateful for your courtesy in informing me by your note of May 5, 1932, of the technical plan which is being considered by the committee of the Canadian House of Commons as a means of providing Canada witfi satisfactory radio broadcasting coverage. You inquire whether the authorities of the United States can make the readjustment necessary to render certain channels available for effective use in Canada.
In reply, I am glad to inform you that as notice is given from time to time of the dates of changes to be made in the present operations of Canadian broadcasting stations t( conform to the plan set out, this government will be glad to make the necessary readjustments.
It is understood that, if as the result of the Madrid conference, any additional channels are made available for broadcasting, a further allocation will be made, as between the United States and Canada, on an equitable basis.
Accept, sir, the renewed assurances of my highest consideration.
W. R. Castle,
Acting Secretary of State.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF CONVENTION FOR SUPERVISION OF INTERNATIONAL TRADE IN MUNITIONS AND IMPLEMENTS OF WAR

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: APPROVAL OF CONVENTION FOR SUPERVISION OF INTERNATIONAL TRADE IN MUNITIONS AND IMPLEMENTS OF WAR
speechtext:
That it is expedient that parliament do approve of the international convention for the supervision of the international trade in arms and ammunition, Geneva, 17th June. 1925, signed on behalf of Canada by the Hon. Raoul Dandurand on the 22nd September, 1925, and that this house do approve of the same.
He said: The international convention for the supervision of the international trade in arms and munitions together with a declaration regarding the territory of Ifni, was drawn up at a conference held in Geneva on June 17, 1925, at which Canada was represented by W. A. Riddell, the Canadian government advisory officer, Geneva.
The convention will enter into force four months after fourteen ratifications have been deposited by the signatory governments with the government of the French republic. So far, thirty-seven countries have signed the convention and thirteen ratifications have been received, but the majority of these are contingent upon ratification iby the producing powers. Of the latter, the following have not yet ratified the convention: Austria, Belgium, Czecho-Slovakia, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States of America. His Majesty's governments in the United Kingdom and in Australia have made their ratification contingent upon ratification iby all producing countries.
The convention was signed for Canada by the Hon. Raoul Dandurand, on September 22, 1925. At this point it might not be inappropriate to read the opening of the convention:
Germany, the United States of America, Austria, Belgium, Brazil, the British Empire, Canada, the Irish Free State and India, Bulgaria, Chile, China, Colombia, Denmark, Egypt, Spain, Esthonia, Abyssinia, Finland, France, Greece, Hungary, Italy, Japan, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxemburg, Nicaragua, Norway, Panama, the Netherlands, Persia, Poland, Portugal, Roumania, Salvador, Siam, Sweden, Switzerland, the Kingdom of the Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, Czechoslovakia, Turkey, Uruguay Venezuela,
Whereas the international trade in arms and ammunition and in implements of war should bp subjected to a general and effective system of supervision and publicity;



Arms and Ammunition Convention
Whereas such a system is not provided by existing treaties and conventions;
Whereas in relation to certain areas of the world a special supervision of this trade is necessary in order to render more effective 'the measures adopted by the various governments as regards both the import of such arms and ammunition and implements of war into these areas and their export therefrom; and
Whereas the export or import of arms, ammunition or implements, the use of which in war is prohibited by international law', must not be permitted for such purpose;
Have decided to conclude a convention and have accordingly appointed as their plenipotentiaries:
The various persons representing the countries I have named.
Who, having communicated their full powers, found in good and due form, have agreed as follows:-
The first article deals with arms, ammunition and implements of war exclusively designed and intended for land, sea or aerial warfare. A description of what is included in that category is found at page 4 of the convention. It divides itself into twelve heads. Probably it would be inappropriate to take up the time of the house in reading them, but roughly they cover all forms of destructive implements and ammunitions, commencing with rifles, muskets and carbines and closing with tanks md armoured cars, and "arms and ammunition not specified in the above enumeration".
Then the convention deals wdth arms and ammunition capable of use both for military and other purposes. That is, it may be used for more than one purpose. Then it deals with vessels of war and their armament; then, with aircraft, assembled or dismantled, and aircraft engines. In category V we find gunpowder and explosives, except common black gunpowder, and arms and ammunition as specified. There is provision as to the supervision and publicity, the relative portions of chapter II reading as follows:
1.	The export shall be for a direct supply to the government of the importing state or, with the consent of such government, to a public authority subordinate to it;
2.	An order in writing, which shall be signed or endorsed by a representative of the importing government duly authorized so to act, shall have been presented to the competent authorities of the exporting country. This order shall state that the articles to be exported are required for delivery to the importing government or public authority as provided in paragraph 1.
Then there are further provisions looking towards the ultimate cessation of production of these weapons of war. I do not suppose however that the house desires me to read those provisions at length. Sufficient to say that having been carefully considered and

signed by our representative in common with the representatives of the other countries I have mentioned, it only becomes effective if as and when the ratifications I have mentioned are made by the producing powers. As a matter of fact all the producing powers have not yet signified their approval, but at this time the matter becomes important by reason of the fact that the disarmament conference is sitting, and it was thought desirable that Canada should not longer await the action of other countries to take the steps I now suggest.
The real truth is that this convention has its origin in the covenant of the League of Nations. It will be recalled that article 23 of the covenant provides:
Subject to and in accordance w'ith the provisions of international conventions existing or hereafter to be agreed upon, the members of the league . . . will entrust the league with the general supervision of the trade in arms and ammunitions with the countries in which the control of this traffic is necessary in the common interest.
On September 10, 1919, before the league had been able to take up the question, a convention for the control of the trade in arms and ammunitions was signed at St. Germain; the object of this convention was to ensure that the large stocks of war material accumulated by the various belligerents should not find their way into unsettled areas where thej' might give rise to trouble. These areas included, particularly, the greater part of Africa and certain regions in Asia, such as Arabia, and the shores of the Red sea and the Persian gulf. The provisions of the convention were stringent. No exports of arms to non-signatory powers was to be permitted and a measure of control under the league of nations was established. This convention, however, proved abortive, mainly because of its non-ratification by the United States who objected to control by a league of which she was not herself a member and to the prohibition of the sale of arms to non-contracting countries.
For several years the league endeavoured to secure the ratification of the convention by the United States and by . other countries, but in September, 1923, the fourth assembly accepted the fact that no further progress in the matter was likely and it instructed the temporary mixed commission-a commission consisting of a number of individuals, and not representatives of states-to prepare a new convention in such a form as might be acceptable to the governments of all countries which produced armaments and they invited the United States to cooperate in this work. The temporary mixed commission pre-

The Late President Doumer
pared a draft which was accepted as a basis for discussion at an international conference which met in Geneva on the 4th of May, 1925. The convention that I have mentioned was the result, and was prepared for signature, on the 17th of June, 1925. As I have just indicated, it has forty-one articles and is divided into five chapters, the object being to establish a general system of supervision and publicity for the international trade in arms and munitions and implements of war, and a special system is set up for areas where measures of this kind are generally recognized to be particularly necessary.
I think I have sufficiently indicated the general purpose of the convention. The summing up of the result of the convention was made by the president of the conference, M. Carton de Wiart of Belgium, in these words:
We are able to present the world with a solid structure not built in the clouds, but founded upon the rock of solid realities. The reduction of armaments 'is not yet achieved, but an important step has been made towards it. For the first time, to use the apt expression of M. Paul-Boncour, the trade in arms is removed from the domain of private law and enters that of public law.
As it now stands the convention has been signed for thirty-seven countries but, as I have already indicated, it has been ratified by but thirteen, and of the countries ratifying it six have made their ratification subject to as yet unfulfilled conditions. The confident hope expressed by the president of the conference seven years ago has not yet been fulfilled, but it should not be said that any part of the responsibility for its failure to enter into force rests upon the Dominion of Canada.
We have not hitherto ratified the convention because independent and isolated action in this field seems futile. Concerted and simultaneous action by the great armament manufacturing countries is not only desirable, but fundamental. If the convention were to enter into force individual governments could hardly be expected to bind themselves to abstain from profitable traffic unless their competitors accepted a similar self-denying ordinance. In these circumstances it seems desirable that Canada should ratify the convention subordinating its ratification to the same condition as that made by His Majesty's governments in the United Kingdom and Australia, that is, the instrument of ratification would include a statement on these lines:
This ratification is subject to the reservation that it shall not take effect until ratifications of the convention shall have become effective, in accordance with article 41, in respect of Austria. Belgium, Czechoslovakia, Germany, Italy, Japan, and the United States of America.
Being, in the language of the convention itself, the great munitions and ammunition producing countries.

subtopic: EXPRESSION OF SYMPATHY WITH THE REPUBLIC OF FRANCE

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXPRESSION OF SYMPATHY WITH THE REPUBLIC OF FRANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the house will agree that it is altogether fitting that before we engage- in- the business of the day we should pause to express our very sincere and heartfelt' sympathy with the Republic of France-a great and friendly power from whose shores the ancestors of so many Canadians sailed centuries ago-in the loss of a well-beloved president, Mr. Paul Doumer, who so tragically met his death by the bullet of an assassin.
President Doumer had celebrated his seventy-fifth birthday and was beloved and revered by all the citizens of the republic. It was, therefore, through no animosity to the man or to revenge a personal grievance that the assassin destroyed so precious a life; nor does it appear to have been the result of a plot planned by an organization to take the life of a great public servant. It was apparently the act of one who in brooding loneliness conceived the idea of assassinating the head of the state and thereby creating confusion and dstrust from which he hoped benefit
271G
fhe Late President Doumer

would accrue to his own country. In view of the repercussions of the act of an assassin in Serbia in June, 1914, one can readily understand the reasons why such hopes might be entertained.
President Doumer had a varied and successful career. He was the architect of his own fortunes and had risen from humble beginnings to become the chief citizen of the republic by the sheer force of his ability and character. In the world of business as well as politics he achieved success without the aid of any of those adventitious circumstances to which public men in the older countries are so frequently indebted. His rise in public esteem was not meteoric. He served in the chamber of deputies, of which he ultimately became the president. He was Governor General of Indo-China for five years, and added to his reputation by the wisdom and prudence of his administration. He was twice Minister of Finance. During the war four of his sons gave their lives for their country. He was elected to the Senate, and it was while president of that body that he was chosen to be the chief executive of the French republic. Although but a short period president, his charm of manner, the benevolence of old age, the sorrow he had endured, and his simple, exact life and democratic conduct of the great office which he held secured for him the affectionate regard of the French people. A lover of peace, a devoted friend and benefactor of those who had survived the conflict of the Great war, as I have said, lie was beloved as a man of the people who interpreted to them the genius of his race.
Canadians of all races and creeds, mindful of the ties of sentiment, both ancient and recent, that connect the national life of our dominion with that of the Republic of France, will sorrow with their citizens in the loss of the distinguished head of their nation, and extend to them the sincere sympathy that springs from long and devoted friendship.
Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING
(Leader of the Opposition): Mr. Speaker, on oehalf of the opposition I should like to join warmly with the Prime Minister in what he has just expressed of appreciation of the character and high attainments of the late President of the French republic, and of the great personal and family sacrifices made by him; and also in what the Prime Minister has said on behalf of the government and people of Canada to the government and people of France by way of sympathy in their great national bereavement. The crime to which reference has been made has shocked '.he entire world, but I think we can honestly
(Mr. Bennett.]
say that in no portion of the globe has that crime served to bring forth a truer expression of sorrow or more genuine sympathy than in this country, which in addition to bonds of friendship is united so strongly by ties of race and language to the Republic of France.

subtopic: AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES RESPECTING MEASURES TO RELIEVE DISTRESS

speechtext: Hon. W. A. GORDON (Minister of Labour) moved the second reading of Bill No. 72, respecting relief measures.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES RESPECTING MEASURES TO RELIEVE DISTRESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
this is the fourth measure to be introduced by the present administration, since coming into oflice, with respect to unemployment relief. The first was the Unemployment Relief Act of 1930; the second was the Unemployment and Farm Relief Act of 1931, the third was the measure passed, a little earlier in this present session, known as the Unemployment and Farm Relief Continuance Act of 1931. The present measure is designated as the Relief Act of 1932.
These various measures have had one characteristic in common; each has departed more widely than the previous one from the observance of the rights and powers of parliament in the matter of legislation, and in turning over those powers to the governor in council. The first measure named the large sum of $20,000,000 for the purposes of unemployment relief, and that sum was appropriated in very general terms. The period for which
that amount was appropriated extended beyond the period of the fiscal year. In those three particulars, in the failure to limit the time for which the amount was voted, the failure to designate specifically the particular purposes for which the money was voted, and the giving to the governor in council of a more or less free hand in the expenditure of public money, over which parliament had little or no control, the legislation was subversive of the rights of this house.
The next measure went a step further by according to His Excellency in council the power to legislate with respeot to peace, order and good government. When the present resolution was introduced, I mentioned that fortunately, and, I believe, wholly., as a result of the strong representations that were made by the opposition against the government usurping the powers of this house in the matter of legislation, that particular provision had not found its way into the measure now before us. But there is a new feature in this measure which will come as a great surprise, especially to those who may not have studied the bill with care. It is that the powers which are given to the governor in1 council-and they are very extensive, going much beyond the mere relief of unemployment-may be exercised notwithstanding the existence of any statute or law. I must confess that I think this is going very far indeed, particularly, when by reading the provisions of the act itself, it is apparent, as I have said already, that the measure relates not merely to the relief of unemployment but also to matters affecting the credit of Canada, even going the length of giving the governor in council power to give financial assistance and guarantees to corporations. That power is a very large one, and who is there who can say to what lengths it may be exercised. The fact that the proposed legislation states that it may be exercised notwithstanding the provisions of any statute or law makes one rather wonder whether all legislation that has been passed by parliament in the ^ast for the protection of the people is not, as far as this provision goes, being wholly over-ridden by the powers we are now asked to confer upon the governor in council.
I have spoken so often of the subversive character of legislation of this kind, that I do not think it necessary to repeat at this time what has been previously said, but by way of emphasis I should like to draw attention to the language of the preamble, which demonstrates as clearly as words possibly could the difference in point of view between those of us who have been opposing certain provisions of
2718	COMMONS
Unemployment

Agreements with Provinces
the several relief measures that have been brought in, and the government which has sponsored them. There has been no difference between us as to the principle of voting unemployment relief. We on this side from the outset have held that we were prepared, subject to the government- advising us that in their opinion certain sums of moneys were necessary for relief purposes, to vote those sums as speedily as could be reasonably expected. We have recognized the necessity of federal relief in an emergent situation, such as exists at present, and we have been prepared to accept the government's word, upon its responsibility, as to the amount which might be necessary to meet the situation. But we have insisted that the government should give some statement to parliament as to the amount necessary, and specifically to designate, as far as might be possible, the objects on which public moneys were to be expended under the act.
May I read the preamble which, while it has little or no value as part of the enactment, nevertheless helps to disclose in terms the intent of the government in regard to the legislation:
Whereas by reason of the prolonged world wide economic depression, recovery to a more normal economic condition has been retarded in the Dominion of Canada; and whereas the provinces require assistance in carrying out necessary relief measures and to meet financial conditions as the same may arise; and whereas it is in the national interest that parliament should support and supplement the relief measures of the provinces and grant them financial assistance in such manner and to such extent as the governor in council may deem expedient; and whereas it is necessary to make special provisions to deal with the situation in the national parks of Canada and in the drought stricken areas of the province of Saskatchewan; and whereas for these and similar purposes the powers necessary to insure the speedy and unhampered prosecution of such relief measures and the maintenance of the credit of the Dominion and the provinces thereof should be vested in the governor in jouncil: Now. therefore. His Majesty, by and vith the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of * Canada, enacts as follows:

The clause in the preamble to which I wish to direct attention particularly is the one which reads:
And whereas it is in the national interest that parliament should support and supplement the relief measures of the provinces and grant them financial assistance in such manner and to such extent as the governor in council may deem expedient.
I cannot more clearly -bring out what we on this side have in mind than by saying that the government in that statement has mistaken the functions of the governor in council

and of parliament respectively. A correct statement of the constitutional position would be that the governor in council, in a matter of this kind, should act in accordance with the wishes of parliament rather than that parliament should act in accordance with the wishes of the governor in council. May I re-read t'he paragraph as it is, and then as I think it ought to read:
It reads:
And whereas it is in the national interest that parliament should support and supplement the relief measures of the provinces and grant them financial assistance in such manner and to such extent as the governor in council may deem expedient.
The paragraph should read:
Whereas it is in the national interest that the governor in council should support and supplement the relief measures of the provinces and grant them financial assistance in such manner and to such extent as parliament may deem expedient.
Parliament is the body that must decide what is expedient and what should be done, and any .power the governor in council may have must be derived from parliament. But here is a statement in the king's English to the effect that it is not parliament that shall decide what ought to -be done, and which gives to the governor in council power to act wit-h an authority with which .parliament alone is vested. In other words, when this clause is read in conjunction with the main enactment of the measure, which gives the governor in council power at his discretion to take from the consolidated revenue fund whatever moneys may be necessary for the purposes of the act, parliament 'becomes simply the endorser of a note which the governor in council may make to any amount for the -purposes named in the legislation.
If that is not subversive of the -powers of parliament, I cannot imagine anything that is; and when we consider that it relates to vast expenditures of -public moneys over which obviously parliament should have complete control, we see how entirely subversive of all the legislative rights and powers of parliament it is.
May I go a step further and direct the attention of the house to another clause of the preamble;
And whereas for these and similar purposes the powers necessary to insure the speedy and unhampered prosecution of such relief measures and the maintenance of the credit of the Dominion and the provinces thereof should be vested in the governor in council.
I submit that the powers that are necessary to ensure the maintenance of the credit of the Dominion and of the provinces are

Unemployment-Agreements with Provinces
powers which are vested, under the constitution, in this -parliament, and that they should not, and legally cannot 'by any enactment of this house, under our constitution as it stands, be transferred, in the words of any statute, to the governor in council, and vested in that body.
A great deal has been said by hon. gentlemen opposite with respect to the supremacy of parliament. They have argued, and I think quite sincerely from their point of view, that parliament is supreme and can make any enactment it pleases. In a broad sense, I admit that unequivocally. But I do submit that there is one difference between the supreme power of the parliament of Canada and the supreme power of the parliament of Great Britain, where the words relating to supremacy would apply without limitation, and that is that in so far as Canada is governed by a written constitution, whatever supreme powers this parliament may have are limited by the terms of that constitution. The constitution may be amended so as to alter or amplify existing powers but so long as they are set forth in specific terms as they are, we are bound by them. In Canada, we are governed, in the main, under the provisions of the British North America Act. Parliament has not the supreme power to go contrary to any provision that is set forth in that act. The British parliament, having no written constitution, might, if it so desired, enact any measure provided it could obtain approval from the majority, and in so doing it would be acting constitutionally. But that is not equally true of this parliament. This parliament has not the power constitutionally to go beyond the terms of the British North America Act with respect to anything in which its powers may be clearly defined therein. These powers, as I have said, it may alter by having the act amended, which it has -power to have done, but it is bound meanwhile by the provisions of the act as they are. In the British North America Act there is a distinct division between the legislative powers, the executive powers and the judicial powers. There is also a clear distinction between the powers of the government with respect to federal matters and with respect to provincial matters. Is there a single member of this house who would suggest that because this parliament is supreme, it would have the right to legislate on any matter coming under the head of t-hose which are exclusively assigned to the provinces? It -would be immediately asserted that we have no such powers because those powers have been assigned to the provinces. In order to bring the matter immediately into relationship with the bill now under
discussion let me ask; would any hon. member suggest that powers -which, under the British North America Act, with respect to legislation are especially assigned to the House of Commons, the Senate and the King's representative could by any statute of this parliament under the act as it stands be vested in the judiciary of this country? I do not think anyone would suggest that. Well, I submit that there is no more power to vest in the executive the legislative powers given under the British North America Act to the House of Commons, the Senate and the King's representative in this country than there is to vest them in the judiciary. All that this parliament can do is, within the limits of its legislative powers, to give certain rights to the governor in council in the nature of administrative powers, but not powers to legislate in the sense in which that power is specifically assigned to parliament by the act. It is the fact that in this proposed enactment the government is taking to itself power not merely to administer laws passed by parliament but to legislate in the stead o-f parliament that causes us to take the exception we do.
What I have just said answers completely whatever hon. gentlemen opposite may say as to the rights of the majority. The majority certainly has rights that can be exercised so long as they are exercised within the terms of the constitution of a country, whether it be written or unwritten. But the majority, simply because it is a majority, has no right to go beyond the language and intent of the written constitution of the land. The same is true with respect to the application of closure in regard to enactments. Closure has a proper place with respect to measures which may be brought before parliament, namely, to see that a measure that is appropriately and properly before the house is not unduly obstructed. But the closure cannot properly be used to prevent a house of commons from seeing that the constitution itself is not being undermined by any measure that may be under consideration. It is because the most important of all the achievements under British government has been the final and complete control of the Commons over all grants that it may make, over taxation, and the right and power of the commons to follow to the last degree the control of public expenditure, that we on this side feel so strongly about not parting with so fundamental a right even, as an exception, in connection with a measure which may relate itself to so important a question as the relief of unemployment. It is not as though the relief of unemployment could not be effected by constitutional means

Unemployment-Agreements with Provinces
quite as well as by unconstitutional methods; it would be all the more effective if it were carried out in a constitutional way.
There is a further reason why at this time, with the knowledge we have of the manner in which this power has been exercised in the last two years, we should be even more guarded in giving it anew to the administration. I shall not go into the different orders in council that have been passed; I shall refer to only one which has already received some discussion in the house and in the committee on railways and shipping. I refer to an order in council whereby a sum amounting to something like one and one-third million dollars was appropriated for the purchase of railway ties. We were told by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) that this was a relief measure carried out under the provisions of the Relief Act. Regarding it as a measure under the relief act, we asked for particulars as to the manner in which contracts for ties had been given, to whom the contracts were given, how much was paid and the like. We were denied by the government the right to obtain the information for which we asked. It was asked for in the form of a return; the government and its followers voted down the motion for the return, and in support of their action the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion) said that this was a matter which came more or less under the control of the Canadian National Railways and that they would not wish the information we were requesting disclosed. Recently the subject came up in the committee of railways and shipping, and there the information which was refused here was asked for. The chairman of the committee, one of the government supporters, gave as his ruling that the information could not be supplied before the committee, but that it could be secured in the house. As his reason that it should not come before the committee, he stated that it could be supplied in the house, though he himself was one of the number who voted against giving the information to the house.
I think I am right in saying that when the matter came before the committee the vote was very close, and it was the vote of the Minister of Railways himself which decided the matter in a way which made it impossible for it to be discussed in the committee.

The right hon. gentleman has made a number of statements which are not correct. I do not say he has made them intentionally, but at the same time they are not according to the facts. At least some of them are inaccurate, and some carry implications which, owing to conclusions which could be drawn from them, might not only do serious damage to the Canadian National Railways but, if correct, would constitute a clear criticism of this government, not in my view, justified by the facts. At first the railways took the attitude that they required no ties. In fact, if the truth is known they bought so many in the two years immediately preceding the election, at a time when my right hon. friend was leader of the government, that they were well supplied, did not require any more, and do not now require them.

Listening to his address and the manner of its presentation, one would conclude that an election was on. Now in the house he plays politics. So far as I am concerned, I shall not play politics, but I like to see people stick to facts.

When I was speaking to the resolution, I explained that in the United States, on the conditions that obtained, it had been found desirable to create a corporation which was authorized to make advances to banks and other financial institutions and corporations and that corporation had a capital of $500,000,000, this amount of course being all subscribed by the United 'States. In fact it is provided that the money itself shall be taken out of the treasury of the United States out of any unappropriated balances, and notwithstanding that fact, it became essential, in order that the operations of the corporation might be continued, that the money should be borrowed. The bulletin of the Federal Reserve Board for April, 1932, contains a full statement of the operations of the finance corporation to date and a short summary that was published by the department gave a clear indication of just how it was proceeding with its work. I need only point out that the statute under which the corporation is incorporated provides, as I have said, for an immediate capital of $500,000,000 being available.
I have endeavoured and, I fear, not successfully, to point out to the house that there is an emergency in Canada as wed as elsewhere in the world. I have tried to the best of my ability to indicate that we are living in the most abnormal conditions under which any people ever lived; that because of the failure *of the first effort to rehabilitate the whole [DOT]financial structure in the life of the world and consequent upon the failure of the Bank of England in September, 1931, to maintain its gold reserves, our position has become very much more difficult than it has been heretofore and that we are in the face of one of the most serious crises which the world has ever known; that Canada with its 10000,000 people inhabiting half a continent, cannot possibly be free from the operations of the great currents that move round about us, currents that make for depression, destruction of values,, almost every peril to which the financial structure of a country could be subjected. I 41761-1721
think it is in the minds of most people that we are living in the most difficult days this country has ever experienced. I believe every thoughtful man who looks below the surface of things, realizes that never before has a greater crisis confronted the Canadian people.
In the face of those circumstances and of that crisis we have suggested that it is desirable that we should foe in a position to do at least what we can to save the credit of Canada and of the provinces and of the whole life, financial and otherwise, of the dominion if the necessity arises. I trust hon. gentlemen realize that other countries some in one way and some in another, are taking the steps we propose to take. I suppose it is in the minds of most who read the papers the other day that the Chancellor of the Exchequer in England set aside a sum amounting to several hundred million dollars for the purpose of protecting exchange. Why? Because the life of Great Britain was threatened nationally and financially', and he desired to protect the structure. The United States is acting in another way. Some countries are repudiating their obligations entirely', and with respect to their external debts they say: We shall not [DOT]pay. And they are not paying. For instance, on Saturday last the securities of a South American republic that sold its bonds at a high price during the last two years, stood at $4 for a $100 bond although the interest rate was six per cent. I give that as an illustration- and I can mention many-of the fact that on these two continents, the North and South American, we 'have a very acute situation, one which is accentuated so far as Canada is concerned, by reason of our juxtaposition, our geographical location to the greatest population inhabiting one area in the world, that population experiencing a condition which is certainly much more difficult, they say, than ours, and however much it may 'be that hon. gentlemen opposite deprecate the actions we have taken, belittle the efforts we have made, and scoff and scorn at what we have endeavoured to do, the fact remains that in the minds of others who are keen and shrewd observers, this country has done very well up to the present. In fact, there are those who think it has done 'as well as, if not better than, any other country in the world.
It may be that misery loves company; it may 'be desirable to say that all the world is in the same position as Canada, and Canada is in the same position as all the world; but to state this is just a common, ordinary everyday fact, and if the measures we suggest fall short of meeting the situation, then indeed we would be blamed. What the leader of the apposition has said is that the government finds itself unable to grapple with this, that or the other problem. When I hear those statements .made and I am reminded of the situation that confronted us in June and July, 1930, I wonder if this is the day of Rip Van Winkle, when men who have been asleep have suddenly wakened up and cannot realize the tremendous world changes that have transpired meanwhile. This government is always willing and ready to accept its responsibilities and to carry them out. But when conditions have changed, when such a crisis as the world has ever known is upon us, I say it is neither fair not does it appeal to the people of this country for a single minute to make comparisons of that kind. What is more, every day brings communications to one member or another of this government, barely a day goes by that I do not personally receive communications from people asking, when they knew this measure was before us, how otherwise could we proceed?
I am not going to labour the point. I have already dealt with it to the best of my ability. I have endeavoured to impress on my fellow-Canadians the gravity of the situation and the extent of the crisis that confronts this country. Hours and days have been taken up in discussing the resolution on which this bill is based. Now we have once more paraded in this house the long and dreary tale of our constitutional wrongs and of the evils that will follow from the application of the principle of this measure. We heard it last year. We have heard it this year three times already. I can almost recite what the right hon. gentleman will say as soon as he gets on his feet. I know that the word "subversive" will be used just as frequently as it is possible for him to use it, and that the word "constitution" will flow from his lips with as much ease as it is possible for words to flow, and you know how easy that is. The constitution is being wrecked, something entirely subversive of the interests of Canada is being proposed, and I cry aloud and none heeds my cry-that is the position of the right hon. leader of the opposition. The whole pillars of the state are being wrecked, and will not one hon. gentleman opposite come to the rescue, come and put down all this tyranny and avoid all the evils that will flow to the Canadian people from this measure

that the government is proposing? That is the position of the right hon. gentleman. Is it any wonder that the people of this country are getting a little weary of that sort of thing and saying that the time has come when men should take action and not indulge in mere words, mere talk about something subversive of the constitution. Oh, the evils that have been wrought in the name of the constitution 1 The right hon. gentleman has never forgotten that a constitutional issue whereby a letter written by the representative of the crown was not made known to the people enabled him to receive power when he should not have had it.

I would not expect the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell) would understand it, but what was done was this, and there the record is, and it stands for itself and can be read of all men. It is not what I say; it is what the record contains. It was a statement written by the right hon. gentleman himself, to which a reply was sent by a representative of the crown, and there are men in this house who went to and fro in Canada in 1926, and I look fairly now at one of them who gave an interview to the Manitoba Free Press in which he spoke of dictatorial powers being used for the purpose of enabling England to trample upon the rights of this country, and that Downing street had suddenly taken the place of Ottawa and dominated the situation in Canada, and that this parliament had not been free to exercise its rights. Read that correspondence. I make no comment; read it. But I do say this, that if the people of Canada had known of that correspondence as they should have, the constitutional issues that we have been hearing about ever since would not have been talked about so often.
Either the right hon. gentleman has become obsessed with this talk about the constitution or else he knows nothing about it-one or the other; for to-day, in dealing with the question of the relative rights of parliament and the executive he exactly reversed the decisions

of the privy council in dealing with those problems. Parliament is all-powerful to deal with our constitutional position, but parliament must delegate its powers to commissions. The railway commission is one. Parliament has appointed that commission and has delegated its powers to it. It has provided how those powers shall be exercised and by whom. Parliament appoints other commissions from time to time and confers upon them the necessary authority for their action. All power must spring from parliamentary action, and when parliament has conferred the power it is determined by parliament who shall exercise that power. Shall it be by a railway commission or shall it be by the executive, and the executive is the governor in council? Parliament is being asked now to confer upon the governor in council, the executive of this countrj-, the power to carry out its will; that is all. When parliament conferred upon the harbour board of Montreal the right to issue securities without limitation and determined that the governor in council might guarantee those securities, if the argument of the right hon. gentleman is right, then every one of those securities is invalid; but everyone knows that they are not invalid, that parliament conferred upon the executive the right to guarantee those bonds without limiting the amount. Parliament was not aware at that time that a few months before the election a couple of millions were to be issued to bring the total up to nineteen and a half million dollars altogether, whereas the representations were that the cost was going to be six million dollars. But parliament conferred the power, and having conferred the power, parliament must be bound by the exercise of it.
In this measure parliament is asked to confer on the executive these powers. I have said, and I repeat, that under conditions so abnormal, in a crisis so great, you will find no case in which there has been any suggestion of corruption or of -wrongdoing within the proper meaning of those words in connection with the exercise of these powers by the governor in council during the last two years. It is true that there are cases in which there are differences of opinion. It is true that there are cases in which there is criticism. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) has dealt with the criticism of the leader of the opposition as to the exercise of the power in granting to the Canadian National a sum of money with which to buy ties for relief purposes. What happened was this: If the Canadian National without our passing an order in council or granting them a single dollar
had gone out and spent money to buy ties, and had then put the cost in as part of its deficit,, as it would have done, and parliament had then voted the money, as it would have done, you would have had exactly the same, identical result. But parliament clothed the executive with power, and the executive in the exercise of that power granted money to the Canadian National to the extent of over one million dollars for the purpose of buying ties, and the Canadian National bought the ties and paid for the ties. It may be that the price paid for the ties was less than it should have been. I have heard it suggested that the price was too low, that it was not a fair price, that a man could not make a living wage making ties at that price. I have heard that suggested by hon. gentlemen on this side and by my hon. friend from Gloucester (Mr. Yeniot) on the other side, and I know when he said it that he meant and believed that the price at which the Canadian National let its contracts for ties was a price not fair to the producer. The Minister of Railways has stated to-day that the price for the ties averaged 52 cents as against a higher price prevailing in days gone by. Mr. Speaker, the principle is that the executive, having been authorized by parliament to make grants for relief purposes, did make that grant to the Canadian National on condition that the money should be expended to buy ties, and the Canadian National bought ties with the money.
It is said that the Minister of Railways indicated that the contracts should all be let to contractors of one political faith, and that in the giving out of relief work it should be kept in mind that all the people of Canada did not belong to one political party. Now as to the extent to which his direction, if you call it that, putting it at the highest, was carried out, it is perfectly pertinent and proper to inquire, but the inquiry must be as to the administration of the railway and not as to the administration of relief. I think all will agree as to that.

I think, sir, Your Honour also said that if the house were prepared to accept a personal explanation which would necessitate my reading the full communication, I might have the privilege of reading it. Of course, if the house denies me that privilege, it has a right so to do; but I really cannot understand why the Prime Minister, of all others, should wish to deny to one who has held the office of Prime Minister, the reading of any communication which is as important in its bearing as this one is, particularly when he himself has quoted only a part of it. If I may then read the communication, it is as follows:
Ottawa, June 28, 1926.
His Excellency
The Right Honourable
The Baron Byng of Yimy, G.C.B., IC.C.M.G., Governor General of the Dominion of Canada, Ottawa.
My Dear Governor General,-
Your Excellency having declined to accept nry advice to place your signature to the order in council with reference to a dissolution of parliament, which I have placed before you to-day. 1 hereby tender to Your Excellency my resignation as Prime Minister of Canada.
Your Excellency will recall that in our recent conversations relative to dissolution I have on each occasion suggested to Your Excellency, as I have again urged this morning, that having regard to the possible very serious consequences of a refusal of the advice of your first minister to dissolve parliament, you should, before definitely deciding on this step, cable the Secretary of State for the Dominions asking the British government, from whom you have come to Canada under instructions, what, in the opinion of the Secretary of State for the Dominions, your course should be in the event of the Prime Minister presenting you with an order in council having reference to a dissolution.
As a refusal by a governor general to accept the advice of a prime minister is a serious step at any time, and most serious under existing conditions in all parts of the British Empire to-day, there will be raised, I fear, by the refusal on Your Excellency's part to accept the advice tendered a grave constitutional question without precedent in the history of Great Britain for a century and in the history of Canada since confederation.
If there is anything which, having regard to my responsibilities as Prime Minister, I can even yet do to avert such a deplorable and, possibly, far-reaching crisis, I shall be glad so to do, and shall be pleased to have my resignation withheld at Your Excellency's request pending the time it may be necessary for Your Excellency to communicate with the Secretary of State for the Dominions.
I am, Your Excellency,
Yours very sincerely,
W. L. Mackenzie King.
I submit that communication makes it quite clear that what I was seeking to do was to avoid the raising of a constitutional issue. I knew that only a short time before a dissolution had been granted to Mr. Ramsay MacDonald at the time he was Prime Minister of Great Britain, after he had been in office for only ten months, and I was sure that any advice which would come from the British government to the then governor general would be to suggest to him to accept the advice of his first minister. This was only one of different courses I suggested with a view of avoiding, if at all possible, the raising of a constitutional issue. It was not done in any attempt to have it appear that the British government were seeking to dominate affairs in Canada. On the contrary I expressly stated at the time that I did not wish even to be informed as to what opinion might come from the British government to the then governor general in answer to any questions in that regard he might submit to the British government.

Another reason will probably be given by the railway. In order to operate the railway economically, locomotives of greater power were necessary, and it had been decided by the directors of the road in the fall of 192S that as soon as the finances of the road would permit, larger locomotives would be purchased in order to enable the Canadian National to compete with other roads. When railway conditions in 1928 and 1929 are compared with the conditions of 1931 it will readily be seen that the time to renew or purchase new equipment was in 1928 and 1929. For instance, in 1929 there were moved on our railroads in Canada 115,187,028 tons of freight, and in the same year 39,070,893 passengers. In 1931, there was a reduction, as compared with 1929, of 41,357,028 tons of freight moved, and of over twelve and a half million in the number of passengers carried. There were employed on our railroads in 1929,
187.846	employees, and in 1931, 154,000, or
33.846	less in 1931 than in 1929. The wages paid to railroad men in 1929 were $290,732,500, as compared with $228,260,000 in 1931, or a reduction in 1931 of approximately $61,500,000. So comparing the number of tons of freight

and the number of passengers moved and the wages paid in 1929 and 1931, it will be realized that the proper time to make purchases, if the' railroad wanted to renew its equipment, was in 1929.
The increased power on the railroads necessitated stronger equipment throughout the trains. The larger the train the greater the danger through weakness in any one part. For instance, in an emergency application of the brakes, a car with a wooden frame is likely to buckle up and cause not only damage to property but possible loss of life. Our railroad record in Canada is second to none in the world. The. records show that our Canadian railroads move approximately twelve thousand tons of freight more per man than do the railroads in the United States. Consequently, Mr. Speaker, I consider that whatever the management wanted to do in the way of keeping up the equipment they had a perfect right to do.
There seems to be a conflict of view between the Prime Minister and the Minister of Railways. While the Minister of Railways did not say so specifically, I understood him to take the view that the railroad management and the government ought to have seen in 1929 that economically things were going wrong in the world and consequently they ought not to have entered upon large purchases, but should have saved the money. On the other hand, the Prime Minister said that no one in 1930 could foresee what the economic conditions of the world might be. However much they differ, I do not think we on this side ought to be compared with Rip van Winkle. No one should deny to the Canadian National Railway, our own railway, the right of keeping the road abreast of other systems on this American continent.
I regarded the Prime Minister's speech this afternoon as a frank confession of failure on the part of his government to meet conditions in this country. He gave as an excuse that no one could foresee in 1930 what the conditions of the world have turned out to be. But I recollect that very many Liberals, as I did myself in some of my speeches on the hustings, blamed conditions in Canada upon world economic conditions. I can recall the then premier of Ontario, the Hon. G. Howard Ferguson, now High Commissioner for Canada in London, making fun of that on platforms throughout northern Ontario. He said it was the Minister of Labour's duty to see that conditions in Canada were all right, and that he should not bother about other parts of the world. I can recall speeches made by the present Prime Minister wherein he stated that

In that year the matter of unemployment was before the people. In no uncertain terms the Prime Minister said it was the duty of the federal government to provide work and that if that government fulfilled its duties there should be no unemployment in Canada. He said a government should find a job for every man and woman able to work, and he undertook to do it. At that time there was no suggestion that it was the duty of the provinces. There was no suggestion that the provinces should take any responsibility, or that the action of the federal government would be merely supplementary. On the contrary the Prime Minister made specific promises that if the Conservative party were elected to power they would end unemployment and treat it on a national basis; there was no question whatever of the provinces coming into the picture. Since that time however, after elected to power, the government headed by the Prime Minister brings in legislation involving provincial obligations. First come the municipalities, then the provinces, with the efforts of the smaller bodies to be supplemented by the federal government. Since the election, therefore, we have witnessed a turn-about-face.
A few days ago the Minister of Labour was answering questions on the national highways matter, and whether or not he endeavoured to evade questions the fact is he was not very frank in his explanations. There are some hon. members on this side of the house wrho would like to know whether or not the government intend to go on with the national highways they promised, or whether they intend only to contribute to the provinces when they are in need. We should like to know the stand now taken by the government. In 1930 no constitutional question was raised. The words of the Prime Minister at Cobourg on June 24 are reported in the London Free Press of June 25 as follows:
A national highway for Canadians. A highway in Canada, not through some other country. A highway in which you can leave Cape Breton and arrive in Vancouver without going into a foreign land. Mr. Bennett declared the undertaking must be accomplished by the hands of the federal government.
At that time there was no question of constitutionality and no suggestion that the provinces would be expected to contribute. A direct promise was made that the national highway would be built, and that promise was one of the weapons used against your humble servant during the last election campaign. Federal Conservatives promised that the highway would be built; the provincial Minister of Lands and Forests and his colleague the then Premier of Ontario, the Hon. G. Howard 'Ferguson, promised from the hustings that the highway would be built. What are we going to do? The Prime Minister has asked for concrete suggestions from this side of the house. The bill now before us provides for only direct relief. If I understand correctly the bill before us, together with the statements made by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Labour, we have nothing in view to-day but direct relief. True, the Ontario government through its Minister of Lands and Forests has stated that there are certain camps in northern Ontario to which anyone who is without a home may go. Those men will be given eight hours' work each day constructing highways, they will be fed and given five dollars a month to boot. That, however, is not a serious attempt to build highways. I am sure the government will not secure men who will be content to work eight hours each day out in the boiling sun constructing highways, and receive in return only five dollars a month.
I should like to know this: Is northern Ontario again to be treated to another period of highways political expediency? The highways in northern Ontario have for years been kept for political expediency. After the money which was spent last year on the highway are we this year simply going to close down those expensive camps? I have no complaint about them, because I do not think anything can be too good for the men in that part of the country. But in view of the expenditures which have been made in camps and equipment, are we going to allow the parts of highways already constructed to grow up in bush and weeds, or are the people in that part of the country to receive the justice which for years they have been seeking?

I am pleased that on many occasions the Prime Minister has acknowledged-that the highways in Canada would be an asset, not a liability. From time to time he has referred to the great value to Canada of the tourist traffic. In northern Ontario we have one of the finest tourist districts to be found anywhere on the North American continent. Lakes, rivers, streams and forests abound, with fish, game and all sorts of possibilities for sport. Only an expenditure of a few thousand dollars is necessary to connect that great portion of the country with western Canada and the United States. The history of the northern highways is one upon which we cannot look with any degree of pride. I can recall that in 1921 the government of the day in Ontario was persuaded to cooperate with the Manitoba government in connecting the provinces of Ontario and Manitoba. In 1921 contracts were let and the work proceeded fairly well until 1923. Then the government changed in Ontario and the work was practically closed down. In 1924 Mr. Lyons, Minister of Lands and Forests, made several speeches in that part of the country and emphatically put his government on record as being determined to complete the highway from the Manitoba boundary to Sault Ste. Marie. Nothing was done except scratching the surface. In the provincial election of 1926 the highway was again promised; in 1926 during the federal election the highway was again promised; but nothing much was done. The Conservative candidate had been elected in the 1926 elections, but at the next provincial election in 1929 the electors declined to accept any further promises, and he was defeated. In the meantime the Manitoba government had gone ahead with the construction of their portion of the highway. Owing to the urgent representations of the present local member in the Ontario legislature, backed by others, the Ontario government did go ahead, and during the federal election of 1930 the provincial Minister of Lands and Forests specifically promised that the highway to Manitoba would be open for traffic in 1931. We have been a little delayed, but now we are assured that it will be ready for traffic by the first of July this year. I gladly take the opportunity to invite every member of this house to be present on that occasion so that they may have the pleasure of visiting one of the finest tourist districts in the whole dominion.
I am hoping that the government will not be a party to the arrangement said to have been made with the provincial government, but that they will undertake to carry out at least one of their pledges to the people, even

if it is only the connecting up of the provincial highways. Sixty-one miles of construction would complete the highway from Ignace to Winnipeg. There are a few miles of uncompleted road here and there; in addition another twenty-nine miles of construction work is needed to complete the highway between Sioux Lookout and the town of Dinorwic and Dryden; then we have a highway under construction to the south connecting up Kenora and the Rainy River districts. In other words, it will take sixty-one miles of road work to complete the main highway, another twenty-nine miles across to Sioux Lookout, and sixty miles across to Rainy River; these will connect up the whole of new Ontario with western Canada and the outside world. Figuring the cost at $S,000 per mile this work can be completed for $1,200,000. I am satisfied that if the Prime Minister and his government will proceed with this highway construction they will be doing something for that part of new Ontario and at the same time they will be creating a national asset and it would be much better to provide work in this manner than by direct relief. I am making the suggestion at this late hour in the hope that the Minister of Labour will see to it that this highway work is proceeded with. On the last occasion when I was speaking on this subject I pointed out to him that it was false economy to go ahead with road construction work in the winter season and then to suspend operations in the summer. Winter temperatures in that country run from 20 to 40 and even 50 degrees below zero. Hon. members will readily understand how hard it is to construct highways under such severe climatic conditions, but the work has been gone on with all winter; now the men are being laid off and put on direct relief, although the camps are fully equipped for continuing the work. The provincial Minister of Lands and Forests, speaking in Kenora in July, 1931, said, according to the Miner and News of July 15, 1931:
Winter work in road building was only carried out to relieve distress. Winter work was a nuisance and a criminal waste for they did not get value for money expended. The men could not possibly give them value under winter conditions.
It will be observed that he bears out what I said on a previous occasion. I think this government will be lax in its duty if they do not undertake to complete that highway now that we have so many men out of work and when it could be proceeded with under conditions which would permit the men to work in comfort and render full value to the country.
