A little while ago I said I did not think the Minister of Labour was altogether frank the other day when I asked him several times in respect to this highway. To say the least he did not give a direct answer. The -provincial Minister of Lands and Forests, however, has made a statement in connection with the matter. It may be that he is wrong ;-if the Minister of Labour says he is I will not quarrel with his statement, for I have often found him wrong-but this is what the provincial minister said as reported in the Kenora Miner and News of April 27 last, the report being copied from the Mail and Empire:
Hon. William Finlayson, Minister of Lands and Forests, announced last night that the plan worked out by the dominion and provincial governments is purely a relief measure to afford shelter for men in the camps who have no other means, many of whom have expressed a desire to stay in the north after the official closing time, rather than coming into the cities.
The men will be given board, lodging and five dollars a month spending money, and will work eight hours daily under the supervision of the permanent engineering staff of the Department of Northern Development. Notification of this arrangement was given to the camps yesterday.	'	.	.If that be true, the Minister of Labour might have been frank enough the other night to say so. I think that when a member from this side asks a question he is entitled to an answer. But I hope it is not true, I hope the Minister of Labour-who belongs to the north country himself, and I know is just as solicitous for its development as I am-I	hope he will not be a	party tothe closing down of the camps and so render more or less useless some portions of the work already done. It is ridiculous to ask workmen to go into that part of the country and labour for five dollars a month. The Hon. Mr. Finlayson wanted to do that over a year	ago,	at that time	he	suggesteda remuneration of fifty cents a day. Apparently he	was	shamed out of	that,	but nowhe does	not	even offer fifty	cents a day.
Five dollars a month is not even twenty-five cents a day, and I hope the present federal government will not be a party to paying men a pittance of five dollars a month and board and lodging. Therefore I beseech the Minister of Labour, the members of the government, and in particular the Prime Minister, to go ahead and carry out what they obligated themselves to do in 1930, and construct the highway through new Ontario.

Their recommendation was
that direct relief, being wasteful and demoralizing, as far as possible should be discontinued in favour of work for which some remuneration could be given. It may be that the word "dole" would not be a good description, but certainly the resemblance is very close. I take it that British Columbia wanted to go on with a policy of providing work rather than a policy of direct relief. However, we will suppose that the policy to-day is to be one of direct relief, so the next thing we want to know is what share of that expenditure is to be borne by this government. I think that question was directed to the minister when the resolution was in committee, and we were told that it had not been decided. That is a very important point. I do not intend to quibble with the government with regard to the constitutional point of view, but here is the government announcing its policy, so surely it would be appropriate to tell us at least what proportion of this direct relief it contemplates paying. Section 2 gives the government power to enter into agreements, but it does not say what percentage shall be borne by the federal authority. We have only the experience of the past to guide us, and we know that last year the cost of direct relief was paid equally by the municipalities, the provinces and the dominion, each paying 33i per cent. Is that plan to be. followed again this year? We do not know, and I think it is highly important that we should know. For one thing it materially affects the interests of the province and of the municipality. Last year they each paid 33i per cent of the cost of direct relief, but in connection with unemployment work the province only paid 25 per cent and the city paid the same. That would make a very substantial difference to the municipalities in my. district, and I am free to say that they cannot pay that proportion this year. It is not fair to compel them to adopt a policy under which, instead of paying less, they will pay more than they paid in the past.
There is another point I should like to raise iu that connection; I do not know that it particularly arose in British Columbia but a case did come under my observation in

connection with a town in Ontario. They exhausted the money available for unemployment relief work; they could have fallen back on direct relief, but they did not want to do so and the men did not want to receive orders for groceries and give nothing for them. So the city allowed them to continue working and paid them by these relief orders, but they were told; either by the province or by the dominion that they would have to discontinue this practice or they would not get the dominion government's share of the cost of direct relief, which was supposed to be limited to the giving of grocery orders to people who were not working. I should like to know if that contingency has been provided for; certainly it should be. The other day I saw that the city of Nanaimo had adopted what seemed to- be a reasonable policy of what they called direct relief. Attached to it was a condition whereby the unemployed people who received these grocery orders worked them out on the basis of $31.50 a month for a married man. This amounted to eight days' work a month, but perhaps there would be the danger that the city, and in its turn the province, would not be eligible to receive the share of the Dominion government, because it might not be called direct relief inasmuch as the men did some work. The minister may tell us that this is not so, but that is what we want to know. We want to know, to put it in the vernacular, where we get off. We want to be able to go home to our municipalities and tell them just what are their rights in the matter.
While my next point is not exactly pertinent to this section I might just introduce it here. Under section 7 the regulations and orders in council made under the provisions of the act are not to be laid before parliament-until the following April 15. These regulations especially, and the orders in council as well, should be made public at the earliest possible moment. By this time the cities of British Columbia have acquired a sort of aloof attitude towards the provincial government; the cities feel that they must be rather careful in their dealings, and they, want to know what are their rights. Within a very few weeks the government must inevitably pass these regulations indicating what their policy is, and I submit that they should be in this bill. Suppose they state the policy in the regulations; then I say that the regulations should not be merely sent to the province to leak out by slow degrees to the people in the districts, but at the very earliest moment they should be published in the Gazette so that everyone would know just where he stood. If they cannot afford to do

This section gives the governor in council the power, on such terms and conditions as may be agreed upon, to:
(a)	Enter into .agreements with any of the provinces respecting relief measures therein;
(b)	Grant financial assistance to any province by way of loan, advance, guarantee or otherwise;
(c)	Take all such measures as in his discretion may be deemed necessary or advisable to protect the credit and financial position of the dominion or any province thereof;
(d)	Loan or advance money to, or guarantee the payment of money by any public body, corporation or undertaking.
The governor in council is given power to do all those things which, in themselves, are very wide. The clause as it reads, however, goes even farther, because it gives the governor in council power to do all those things "notwithstanding the provisions of any statute or law." In other words, all the laws or statutes this parliament may have enacted which relate to any of the matters dealt with bjr this section may be set aside by the governor in council, if in entering into agreements, making loans or advances under this section or in dealing with other matters referred to he so decides. Subsection (d), to which reference has just been made, is as follows:
Loan or advance money to, or guarantee the payment of money by any public body, corporation or undertaking.
That includes loans, guarantees or advances to banks, trust companies, insurance companies, investment companies, transportation companies, construction companies. The section as it reads means that any of these bodies if large enough, may receive public moneys in the form of loans, guarantees or the like at the discretion of the governor in council, notwithstanding the provisions of any statute or law which may have been enacted by this parliament to safeguard public interests in any dealings with corporations such as I have mentioned. I should like to hear from the minister his justification for those words. Instead of the words of "notwithstanding the provision of any statute or law' I think there should be substituted "subject to the provisions of any statute or law." I think the hon. gentleman misunderstood what I said this afternoon; perhaps I was not speaking sufficiently loud to be heard. What I intended to say, and what I think I did say, was that this was intended to take the place of such a corporation. I stated that in the United States they had incorporated a finance corporation with a capital of $500,000,000, and when the resolution was before the house some time ago I pointed out what had been done in other countries. This afternoon I instanced the action of the Chancellor of the Exchequer in England in connection with exchange; I pointed out that some countries in South America had defaulted in the payment of interest on their external debt, and I stated that this was the case in other countries as well. This clause is intended to enable the government, instead of creating a corporation, all the capital stock of which it would hold, to make such advances to public enterprises or undertakings as may be necessary in the interests of the well-being of this country as a whole. Undoubtedly that is what is intended. There is no doubt that the provision is broad, but it is not so broad as what is now being done by the finance corporation in the United States, and I think it only fair to say to the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth that I was endeavouring to avoid what I think he will agree it is desirable we should avoid, namely the creation of an organization for the purpose of doing just what the finance corporation is doing in the United States, relieving institutions of their difficulties in connection with frozen assets. Perhaps the hon. gentleman knows better than I do what would happen if we had such a corporation in this country; it would be asked to accept all the wildcat securities there were in Canada, and that I desire to avoid.
Without going into any very great detail I think it is not unfair to say to this committee that I do not suppose there is one member who does not realize that a condition might arise-and some prophets of gloom say it will arise-in which it may be most desirable in the interests of this country as a whole that we should prevent attacks upon our credit such as would bring about the results we have seen in the United States, where in two years some four thousand banks failed and innumerable trust and deposit organizations were compelled to close their doors, with a
reorganization possible only by regard being had to the provisions of the finance act. I was told what I believe to be the truth, that half a billion dollars will not be sufficient for the purpose but that much larger sums of money will be required. We have not inexhaustible sources of supply, and it is my conviction that this clause is preferable, in the interests of the country and the orderly conduct of its business, to the creation of a corporation with power to do what the finance corporation is doing in the United States.
I can see how the hon. gentleman misunderstood what I said this afternoon. I was comparing what has been done in the United States with what we were endeavouring to do, and I suggested that the method we are adopting is preferable to the method wdiich has been adopted in that country. In every case the public weal must be the determining factor, and the effect upon the national credit must be the matter that will influence any government in taking whatever action it may desire to take in the premises.

Mr. Chairman, I confess to the hon. gentleman that I would find it difficult to answer his question antecedently to the event. If a situation arose in this country in which I believed it desirable from a national standpoint to assist any public enterprise, which is defined as meaning an enterprise with more than thirty-five shareholders, I would not hesitate to recommend that th's should be done. I say that very

frankly to my hon. friend. But the test must be the necessity of the case, and the necessity of the case must, in turn, be determined not only by the immediate effect upon the enterprise itself, which is not the primary consideration, but by the effect upon the country as a country. I need hardly say to the hon. gentleman that there are contingencies that might arise in this country, if the prophets of gloom are correct, that have no relation to the resources or the strength of the enterprises or institutions inherently; but because of, shall I say, panic conditions in other parts of the world, the immediate effect might be so great as to render it desirable to bolster them up for the moment with the public credit of this country. That is the purpose of it, and I put it to this committee whether it is more desirable to create an institution, just as was done in the United States, in which we should have to find the money to enable it to function and name two or three men as board of governors to do it. It might be done in that way, and it is not improbable that we should find ourselves in a position of very great difficulty by reason of the facts to which I have just alluded.
My best judgment is this-and I am not seeking to impose my judgment on the committee: I can only say frankly that I have given this phase of the matter much more thought and consideration than any other branch of the bill in consequence of what has been communicated to me by persons living outside of Canada who have endeavoured, with some degree of success, to impress upon me the fact that we may be faced with extremely difficult conditions on this continent during the next few months. International transactions of a large character have been carried on by this country in the past and we are not living solely to ourselves; and it might be desirable, in the judgment of those whose opinion I respect, that we should have some power such as this. Because I have myself a strong desire to be in a position to protect the credit and the safety of the financial structure of the dominion and of the provinces, this power is sought. I am only giving my private opinion when I say that unless I felt that the effect upon the country of any particular enterprise-using the word which I think my hon. friend used-being permitted to become insolvent or bankrupt -unless, I say, the effect of that upon the public, or upon the welfare of this country -perhaps that is a better word-were apparent, I should hesitate to recommend that the power should be used. If, on the other hand, the evidence of that result were there, I do not think any government could hesitate IMr. Bennett.l
at a time like this to ask for its use and to use it.	.
I am afraid I cannot usefully give any more extended explanation except to say that in connection with Beauharnois I cannot recall that it has ever been suggested that the power should be invoked for that purpose. But if the necessity became sufficiently great the power would be employed for that purpose. I think it is only fair to answer the question that way, although that is not the purpose for which the power is put there. It is put there to meet a situation which I am bound to say one of my most valued colleagues strongly thinks could best be met by establishing a finance corporation. But my own judgment, my conviction is very strong that it would not serve the purposes we have in mind at this time to create any such institution. I am afraid I have gone as far as I reasonably could without putting myself in a position where I might find it difficult to reconcile my statement with the necessity that might arise; and if the necessity arises I do not desire to be limited either by any antecedent promise or by any restriction of interpretation upon the power here conferred.

I do not think anyone desires to embarrass the Prime Minister by asking for a more lengthy explanation. With respect to the clause itself, I suppose that those of us on this side of the house who think that the government has already taken sufficient power might oppose it; but I will agree with the Prime Minister that there is room for very wide divergence of opinion as to the method which he proposes to follow in loaning or advancing moneys. I suppose the Prime Minister has given-in fact he says he has-very careful thought to this matter, but it would appear to me and, I believe, to a great many of us, that the opinion of his valued colleague, to the effect that it would be 'better to have some kind of finance corporation or some kind of commission to deal with matters of this sort, would perhaps be worthy of more consideration than appeal's to have been given it.
The Prime Minister realizes better than anyone else does the amount of work which the members of his cabinet will have to do. They will be employed during a good part of the summer dealing with problems arising out of the imperial conference. It seems to me that it would be only the fair thing to relieve themselves of this burden, and they would be giving the best thought and consideration to matters of this kind if they set up some kind

of commission-iand I am not saying that because I personally approve of commissions, for I think we have too many already. But this is possibly the most important section of the bill. The Prime Minister must be aware that, by inserting a clause of this kind, he is substituting himself and his government, and the Minister of Finance, I have no doubt, for a commission. All sorts of applications will be made for the backing and guaranteeing of wildcat schemes such as he has referred to, and I have, no doubt the government have the strength of character to refuse these applications. On the other hand, it seems to me that the Prime Minister and the members of his government, or the treasury board,-I assume that they will be dealing with these matters- are taking on themselves a most intolerable burden. There are institutions in this country, there are public corporations and companies which are in urgent need of financing, and after hearing or reading the Prime Minister's statement of to-night they will, I have no doubt, be camped on his doorstep to-morrow. Personally I would suggest that this power and authority be curtailed somewhat, even if the minister were to accept an amendment, that such advances or loans should not be made unless they were in the interests of unemployment relief. The credit of the country can already be sufficiently protected by steps taken under clause (c), which declares that the governor in council may:
Take all such measures as in his discretion may be deemed necessary or advisable to protect the credit and financial position of the Dominion or any province thereof.
It seems to me that is going pretty far; it is going almost far enough. If we are going to protect the credit of private corporations, I very respectfully suggest that that is a power that should not be in the hands of a political body such as the ministry.

In last year's act. paragraph (c) of section 3 read as follows:
Assist provinces, cities, towns, municipalities, and other bodies or associations, by loaning moneys thereto or guaranteeing repayment of moneys thereby, or in such other manner as may be deemed necessary or advisable.
Under the provisions of that statute moneys were loaned .to four of the provinces and in respect to another an undertaking was made which happily had not to be carried into effect. No loans were made to municipalities, because we took the ground that there was no contact between municipalities and the dominion. If the hon. gentleman reads the clause to which he has just referred, he will observe that it covers cases dealt with partly
in paragraph (c) of Section 3 of the statute of last year,, and also special provisions with respect to the provinces themselves.
I do not fear any camping upon the doorstep of the government by any enterprises, because the government has no intention that this power shall be utilized except under the circumstances that I have indicated. This power under paragraph <c) has been referred to on more occasions than one, but we have not yielded to such requests, nor have we any intention of doing so. I may say, however, that unless conditions were emergent, we should not have this bill before the house at all, and it will be borne in mind that when this afternoon we were discussing the nice division of power between the provinces and the dominion, their lordships of the privy council, speaking in connection with the regulation of paper prices, were good enough to say that there may exist in this country an emergency under which the powers of the provinces must be subordinated to, must be overborne by that of the dominion, for the national good.
In this instance, subject to whatever limitations may be imposed upon an executive by reason of a sense of the gravity of a situation and the responsibility they owe to the people at large, I know of no other way in which, without creating an invitation for the government to undertake to liquefy vast volumes of securities that are now frozen-which action it has no desire or intention of taking -we can accomplish what we have in mind. And because we desire to utilize these powers only where the national good is affected, although it may be charged that this is a political body, I should like to remind the committee that it is a political body which every year determines just what advances shall be made under the Finance Act to the banks of this country. It may be political, but I am only saying that is so and has been for years, yet I have not heard anyone say that this power has been exercised for political consideration. Every year the Minister of Finance and the treasury board must consider to what amount advances under the Finance Act shall be made to the chartered banks of Canada. The banks make their applications; they are rarely granted in full. The government, that is the treasury board, determines what action it shall take and grants the credits accordingly. No greater power is involved in the exercise of what is provided for under this clause than is provided for under the provisions of the Finance Act and the Bank Act, and I have not heard it charged that this political body has for political considerations exercised that power.

I only desire to make this further observation. With the closing words of my hon. friend from Shelburne-Yarmouth I have no quarrel. It was Jefferson who said that government was best conducted that interfered the least with business, and it was a great American who coined the phrase:	He
governs best who governs least, with respect to business. Business is not the function of government. I have publicly and privately expressed that opinion so frequently that I suppose it is well known to everybody. I do not believe it is any duty of a government to conduct the business of this country, and were it not for an emergent condition in which the national interest is affected it would not be even considered or mentioned so far as I am concerned.
With respect to what the hon. gentleman has just now said as to the method by which it is proposed to give effect, if effect is given, to the authority thus conferred upon the executive, I think in the very nature of things it would be done through the institutions of the country. No one is expecting that John Smith's company is going to come up and ask for a loan and get it, and if that is what the hon. gentleman is worrying about I can assure him that no one is going to deal with the matter in that way. My hon. friend is now discussing another phase, namely the method by which it would be done. I fancy if some of my colleagues were to tell the hon. gentleman exactly what my views are as expressed he would have no difficulty in learning, as naturally anyone with any experience at all would realize, that it would not be a proper exercise of power except in the most exceptional circumstances to undertake to make a loan to an enterprise as such, but one would through the constituted channels of business give effect to the provisions of the statute. When I say constituted channels of business I mean what the hon. gentleman is referring to, the banks and various other financial
institutions that have to deal with the question of finance and credits. I am not unmindful, in fact, I have too much knowlf edge of what the hon. gentleman says as to the undesirability of governments trying to conduct business. I am having it brought home to me almost every day by the demands that are being made to meet the obligations which we have guaranteed of various enterprises simply because we found ourselves in business. Last week, for instance, it was the Montreal harbour commission in connection with the bridge; or it is the Quebec harbour commission; the Three Rivers harbour commission; the Chicoutimi harbour commission; the Halifax harbour commission; the St. John harbour commission. All these do not have their securities maturing on the same day, and the obligations are being constantly thrust upon us. There are others that might be mentioned. No one would think for a minute, if that is what the hon. gentleman has in mind, that one would desire to add to his responsibilities, or that any member of the government desires to add to his responsibilities by endeavouring to conduct the business of other people whose special knowledge should enable them to conduct it better than anyone else could. But there are enterprises in this country that are as much a part of this country as the country itself. There are great enterprises in this country to which references have been made in this house during the last few months. No one could contemplate disaster overtaking some of them, as the hon. gentleman himself said some evenings ago, without using every possible effort to prevent it. One does not know what may happen. I am not endeavouring in any sense to alarm this house, but I do know that every day one hears further tales of a situation that is not blamable to Canadians nor yet to a Canadian situation, but which obtains by reason of our relation to world business and world enterprise. I can assure the hon. gentleman that so far as I am able to control it, I should not endeavour to utilize these powers by direct action between the enterprises themselves and the dominion except, for instance, in a case such as he has mentioned, in the case of the Beauharnois undertaking-I did not think of it until he mentioned it-where the canal is completed and provides for navigation facilities, and for the sake of continuing the enterprise we acquire the bonds or short term notes, whatever they might be, that represent the cost of the navigation undertaking. That would merely mean a temporary loan pending the financing of the organization in accordance

But as to the methods to be employed to accomplish that end I have not given any thought to it: I do assure my hon. friend and this committee that no man who. has had any experience in business in Canada under present conditions would think of endeavouring to have the government conduct business as such, but would look to the constituted organizations. and institutions created by this parliament and otherwise for the purpose of dealing with these matters, feeling a sense of security in so doing and using entirely their own judgment in connection with the matter.
As an illustration I once more refer to a matter very painful to discuss, and that is the Manitoba savings office. It was just because we had no facilities to engage in the business of banking that we were not able to take over that enterprise. We had no facilities for that purpose, and all we could do was to utilize the existing facilities. One of two things had to be done. It was suggested that we take it over and say: Everything is safe, we will guarantee and take the business over. But we had nobody to put in the office. The office had to be continued or else closed, and I certainly gathered that it was intended to close it. It it were closed it would naturally be taken over by the only institutions that this country has to deal with that business, namely, the banks. The banks divided these deposits of about 40,000 people and became responsible for the payment to them of their deposits. All they had as security until we came into the picture were pieces of paper signed by the province of Manitoba, which had exhausted all its collateral securities, by sale or hypothecation, and which had left as security no money but only pieces of paper belonging to the province. They called them exchequer bills, and under those circumstances, just as the hon. member has pointed out, the banks said, "We will not add to our present securities of that kind; in fairness to our depositors and our business, we cannot. "But," they said, "if you will say that we are not going to be losers in this transaction, we will take over those deposits"-and we did. That is an illustration of the similarity of views between the hon. member and mj'self.

Therefore there could have been no difficulty in understanding that the government had declined to me.et that request. It has declined as courteously as possible; it has declined as firmly as possible; there was opportunity for neither ambiguity nor misunderstanding. They simply said, "no" as politely as it could be S&id. I am sure it was said as politely as any observations made by the hon. member for Melville in this or any other session.
That being so, the hon. gentleman says that the north and south have been treated differently, and he makes the further statement that the bonus resulted in some receiving large sums of money; he mentions the sum of $1,000. The bonus was paid for one reason, and for one reason only, namely that the cost of production exceeded the cost obtainable for the grain, owing to the depressed conditions throughout the world. I do not know, but I am told by one of the prime ministers in the west that had it not been for the intervention of the federal government the price of wheat would have fallen to forty cents a bushel. Whether that statement is correct or not I cannot say.
So far as those in authority is concerned,
I wish to go further and state that when we made provision for the bonus the crop reports were somewhat different from the actual returns, and the crops in the north were much more favourable than had been anticipated. In other words there was a larger crop harvested in the west than was expected at the time we took action, and I am very glad that was so. I do not think any of those who received the bonus find themselves so rich that they have had difficulty in disposing of their money. In the south, where the crop was a partial failure, the government was called upon to make very substantial contributions. The hon. member will no doubt recall that in cases fifty per cent and in one or two cases sixty per cent was paid either by way of direct assistance, or otherwise, to enable those who had gone two years without a crop, or with only half a crop, to find themselves in a better position. It does not follow that this seeming inequality resulted in as great hardship as would appear; in fact the hardships were not nearly as great as they appear when stated. I think I can say I have answered the hon. gentleman's question, and I am sorry he was not aware of the answer that was given some months ago.

That is quite-satisfactory. I do not say-the solution is satist-factory, but at least we have had a stater ment, and that is the first time such a statement has been made in my hearing in this house. The last statement was made by the Minister of Agriculture, and was very plausible. He took the ground at that time -and I think he was justified-that inasmuch hs there were certain adjustments to take place between the dominion and the province of Saskatchewan a definite answer could not be given until the end, of the fiscal year. So far as the delegation is concerned, may I say they went back home and had nothing but good things to say about the way the Prime Minister had received them. He gave them everything but an assurance that they would receive the bonus. They were not turned down, however; there was still hope of some alternative, or something to come in the following year. They certainly did not consider they had been turned down flat. Now, however, when we know the situation, we will not persist any longer. I know the policy of the government, and I shall not discuss the relative merits of the two kinds of treatment. At a later time when I shall have something to say, I shall know my ground.
Perhaps now at this time we could get some information concerning the promissory notes. The hon. member for South Battleford asked one or two questions, but the Minister of Immigration seemed to shy a little bit from an exhaustive or definite answer. The people of Saskatchewan do not want to be beggars, but at the same time if there is going to be a dole policy in all other -parts of the dominion and a promissory note policy in Saskatchewan, why the discrimination? Why should we be thrown into the hands of the Saskatchewan government subject to whatever action they wish? When we ask this government what it means they disclaim any responsibility in the matter. I should like to have a statement from the Prime Minister- that is good enoungh for me. If he tells us that the government will continue the promissory note plan with the Saskatchewan farmers and the same if there is any further seed to be obtained, and if he will say that they are not going to insist upon that policy in any other part of the dominion, we will know then what opinions to form of the disparity between policies-between	the treatment
Saskatchewan gets and that given to the balance of the dominion.

Mr. Chairman, the provision for the taking of seed grain liens for

seed grain advances is a matter wholly determined by the provinces of Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan. I only know we were assured that they were by appropriate legislation making provision in that regard. As to the details of it, I am not in a position to speak because the government did not believe it had, for the reasons given this afternoon by the leader of the opposition, the right to ask the provinces how they did their business. Saskatchewan, Manitoba, and Alberta borrowed from the dominion government money to pay for seed grain, and that seed grain was sold to their citizens-that is my advice-and for that they took a statutory lien specially provided for by the respective legislatures. My memory is that having told us they proposed to do that we merely said: We assume you are taking the security that you mentioned-because part of it was verbally said-in this regard. I do recall that one province proposed that the seed should be paid for within one year, and some I thmk within two years. The details of that each province has to work out itself. I am bound to say I have not even seen the bill that was passed by any one of the three provinces to deal with this matter. They have all been treated on the same basis, and they are the only provinces thus far that have sought advances from the dominion to buy seed grain. It is not the obligation of this government to supply seed grain; when those provinces were part of the Northwest Territories it was, for then they were wards of the dominion. Every province stands in the same position, and none other than three western provinces has asked for money with which to buy seed grain. That is so far as my memory serves me at the moment. The advances that they desired were very substantial. For those advances they gave us treasury bills to the extent of one hundred cents on the dollar. As they are only permitted to give treasury bills for a year at a time, I think they were all payable one year from date, with interest at the same rate as that at which we borrow money.

Before we take up section 3 I want to get an answer to my question. Ever since last year until quite recently the commission in Regina has been extolled from the housetops as being the most wonderful institution of its kind. Now we find nobody around here wants to speak a word for it? What has happened? Can't we get something more about what it is doing and who is responsible for it? We know who appointed the commission; of course the Saskatchewan government appointed it, but there are three supervisors, and we would like to know more about them; we understand they were appointed by the Minister of Agriculture. Then we have a super-superviser in the person of Percy Gordon, and we would like to know more about his duties. We want to know first if this is to be a dole all over the dominion with the exception of Saskatchewan, 41761-1741
and if Saskatchewan is to be expected to pay back everything it gets. Are they all to be treated alike or are they not? Is the government to hold itself responsible in any measure at all for the policy of the Saskatchewan relief commission, or are we to be thrown into the maw of this commission and just take what we can get? I do not want to be too insistent about this, Mr. Chairman, but please do not call this section carried until we get a more specific answer with regard to these promissory notes which the Saskatchewan farmers have to give for everything they get. The Minister of Immigration knows that I asked these questions last Friday. I did not request a reply; I asked him to discuss these questions with his colleagues over the weekend and try to give us a reply later. I said it as nicely as I could, but we are still without a reply.

This government had nothing whatever to do with it beyond supplying the money, for which we obtained the treasury bills of the province, to enable them to purchase the grain sold to the farmers. My understanding of the bill, which I have not read, having seen only what was said to be in the bill, is that it provides for payment out of the proceeds of the crops of this year and next year of the moneys advanced for seed grain and other purposes. Is that a clear statement of the situation? The province borrowed the money and with it bought seed which it sold to the farmers of Saskatchewan, obtaining therefor statutory liens which were adopted at the last session of the legislature. That is the position.

By his observations my
hon. friend has indicated that he was asking questions with regard to which he enlightened this house himself, and for which he takes great credit. We have now to deal with the other question, that of promissory notes for relief given last year by the commission, and continued. Some months ago I explained to the house as clearly as I could that these notes were taken by the commission. In consequence of statements which were made I inquired and found that the commission had taken notes from all persons who received relief, and that the notes were made payable to the crown in the right of the dominion. The hon. member for Weyburn showed me one of the notes, the first I had seen; he sent it to me across the floor of the house. I said further that those notes were taken, as I understood it, because many of the applicants for relief said they did not wish to be in the position of receiving charity, and as a consequence they gave notes. In practice it has been found very excellent in preventing abuses. In other words, by giving a note, whether or not they ever intended to pay it, at least they placed a limitation on what they were receiving, and I can only say further that in one or two cases in which there were abuses, to which I directed attention some weeks ago in this house, it will be remembered that relief had been obtained (Mr. Motherwell.]
by some who were not entitled to it, and the very notes they had given formed the foundation upon which appropriate action could be taken.
I can only repeat to the hon. gentleman that notes haye been given payable to the crown in the right of the dominion. These are printed forms which have not been departed from by the commission that took the notes. So far as I know, notes have been taken by the commission, wdiether or not in all cases I cannot say, but certainly in the cases to which reference was made when we were discussing this matter some weeks ago. We can neither add to nor detract from that fact; notes have been taken and given. They are payable to the crown in the right of the dominion. The commission asked for and received the notes; those who received benefits gave the notes as indicating the extent to which those benefits were received, whether in the w.ay of provisions, clothing, or whatever it might be, in consequence of the orders given by the commission.
